                                            The Galois Alperin weight conjecture for finite category algebras
                                                                                    Xin Huang




                                          Abstract
                                          Let p be a prime, k an algebraic closure of Fp and Γ the Galois group Gal(k/Fp ). Let




arXiv:2604.06166v1 [math.RT] 7 Apr 2026
                                          C be a finite category and OC the p-orbit category of C defined by Linckelmann [4]. We
                                          formulate a version of the Galois Alperin weight conjecture (GAWC) for finite category
                                          algebras stating that there exists a Γ-equivariant bijection between the set of isomorphism
                                          classes of simple kC-modules and that of the weight algebra W (kOC ). We show that the
                                          versions of the GAWC for finite groups and for finite categories are in fact equivalent. If C
                                          is an EI-category, we can give a partition of weights of kOC with respect to blocks of kC and
                                          formulate a blockwise Galois Alperin weight conjecture (BGAWC) for C. We show that the
                                          versions of the BGAWC for finite groups and for finite EI-categories are equivalent.
                                          Keywords: Alperin’s weight conjecture, Galois automorphisms, category algebras, blocks


                                          1. Introduction
                                              The (blockwise) Galois Alperin weight conjecture, due to Navarro [7], a strong form
                                          of Alperin’s weight conjecture [1], predicts that the fields of values of irreducible Brauer
                                          characters (of a block) of a finite group can be locally determined. In this paper we extend
                                          the (blockwise) Galois Alperin weight conjecture from finite groups to finite categories.
                                              Throughout this paper we fix a prime number p and an algebraic closure k of Fp and
                                          denote by Γ the Galois group Gal(k/Fp ). A category C is called finite if its morphism class
                                          is a finite set.
                                              Let C be a finite category. According to [4, Definition 1.1], the p-transporter category of C
                                          is the finite category TC defined as follows. The objects of TC are the pairs (X, P ) consisting
                                          of an object X of C and a not necessarily unitary p-subgroup P of the monoid EndC (X).
                                          For any two objects (X, P ) and (Y, Q), the morphism set HomTC ((X, P ), (Y, Q)) is the set
                                          of all triples (s, P, Q) where s : X → Y is a morphism in C satisfying s = s ◦ 1P = 1Q ◦ s and
                                          s ◦ P ⊆ Q ◦ s. The composition of morphisms in TC is induced by that in C. The identity
                                          morphism of an object (X, P ) in TC is (1P , P, P ). If no confusion arise, we will denote
                                          a morphism (s, P, Q) in TC again by s. Allowing nonunitary subgroups P of EndC (X) in
                                          the definition of objects of TC means that the unit element 1P of P need not be equal
                                          to IdX but can be any idempotent endomorphism of X. The condition s = s ◦ 1P =
                                          1Q ◦ s in this definition implies that HomTC ((X, P ), (Y, Q)) can be identified to a subset of
                                          1Q ◦ HomC (X, Y ) ◦ 1P . With this identification, the morphism set HomTC ((X, P ), (Y, Q)) is a
                                          Q-P -subbiset of 1Q ◦ HomC (X, Y ) ◦ 1P with respect to the actions induced by precomposing
                                          with morphisms in P and composing with morphisms in Q. The condition s ◦ P ⊆ Q ◦ s in
                                                                                         1
the above implies that Q ◦ s ◦ P = Q ◦ s; that is, any Q-P -orbit in HomTC ((X, P ), (Y, Q))
is in fact a Q-orbit. According to [4, Definition 1.2], the p-orbit category of C is the finite
category OC defined as follows. The objects of OC are the same as those of TC . For any two
objects (X, P ) and (Y, Q) of OC , the morphism set HomOC ((X, P ), (Y, Q)) is the set of all
Q-P -orbits Q\HomTC ((X, P ), (Y, Q))/P of morphisms in TC . The composition of morphisms
in OC is induced by that in TC .
    For a finite-dimensional k-algebra A, denote by S(A) the set of isomorphism classes of
simple A-modules. Following [6], given a finite category C, the isomorphism classes of simple
kC-modules are parametrised by isomorphism classes of pairs (e, T ), with e an idempotent
endomorphism of some object X in C and T a simple kGe -module, where Ge is the group of
all invertible elements in the monoid e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e. Such a pair (e, T ) is called a weight if
the simple kGe -module T is in addition projective. The associated weight algebra W (kC) is
an algebra of the form W (kC) = c · kC · c for some idempotent c which acts as the identity
on all simple kC-modules parametrised by a weight and which annihilates all other simple
modules; we review this in Section 3 below. The group-theoretic version of Alperin’s weight
conjecture in [1] is equivalent to the following statement:
Conjecture 1.1 (Alperin [1]). For any finite group G, there exists a bijection between S(kG)
and S(W (kOG )).
   Linckelmann [4] extended Conjecture 1.1 to finite categories:
Conjecture 1.2 (Linckelmann [4, Conjecture 1.3]). For any finite category C, there exists
a bijection between S(kC) and S(W (kOC )).
    In [4, Corollary 1.5], Linckelmann showed that Conjectures 1.2 and 1.1 are in fact equiv-
alent.
Notation 1.3. Let A be a finite-dimensional Fp -algebra and let A′ := k ⊗Fp A. Let σ ∈ Γ.
We see that σ induces an Fp -algebra automorphism of A′ sending x ⊗ a to σ(x) ⊗ a for
any x ∈ k ′ and a ∈ A. We abusively use the same symbol σ to denote this Fp -algebra
automorphism. Clearly Γ permutes the set of (primitive) central idempotents of A′ . For
any A′ -module U , denote by σ U the A′ -module which is equal to U as a k ′ -module endowed
                                          σ
with the structure homomorphism A′ −      → A′ → Endk′ (U ). Note that if f : U → V is an
A′ -module homomorphism, then f is also an A′ -module homomorphism σ U → σ V . Clearly
σ
  U is a simple A′ -module if and only if U is simple. Now we see that the group Γ acts on
the set S(A′ ). Moreover, if b is a central idempotent of A′ , then Γb (the stabiliser of b in Γ)
acts on the set S(A′ b).
   In [7], Navarro predicts a Galois refinement of the Alperin weight conjecture for finite
group which can be reformulated as follows:
Conjecture 1.4 (Navarro [7]; cf. [9, Conjecture]). For any finite group G, there exists a
bijection S(kG) → S(W (kOG )) commuting with the action of Γ.
   This leads to the obvious extension to finite categories:
                                               2
Conjecture 1.5. For any finite category C, there exists a bijection S(kC) → S(W (kOC ))
commuting with the action of Γ.

    If we forget the action of Γ, then Conjecture 1.5 returns to Linckelmann’s Conjecture 1.2.
Similar to Linckelmann’s result [4, Theorem 1.4], we show that Conjectures 1.4 and 1.5 are in
fact equivalent. This equivalence holds more generally for twisted group algebras and twisted
category algebras with a 2-cocycle in Z 2 (C; F×   p ) which is extendible to the orbit category.
There are canonical functors from C to TC and OC sending an object X in C to (X, {IdX }),
and a morphism in C to its obvious images in TC and OC , respectively. In particular, every
2-cocycle α in Z 2 (OC ; F×                                 2     ×
                          p ) restricts to a 2-cocycle in Z (C; Fp ), again denoted by α.

Theorem 1.6. Let C be a finite category and α ∈ Z 2 (OC ; F×    p ). If for any idempotent
endomorphism e in C, there is a Γ-equivariant bijection S(kα Ge ) → S(W (kα OGe )), then
there exists a Γ-equivariant bijection S(kα C) → S(W (kα OC )).

   This will be proved in Section 3.

Corollary 1.7. Conjectures 1.4 and 1.5 are equivalent.

Remark 1.8. (i) In Theorem 1.6, the reason why we require α to be a 2-cocycle with
coefficients in F×                                   ∼
                 p is that in this case we have kα C = k ⊗Fp (Fp )α C, and then the Galois group
Γ has an action on S(kα C) as described above.
   (ii) Note that the formulation in Theorem 1.6 for twisted category algebras requires
the 2-cocycle α to be the restriction to C of a 2-cocycle of OC along the canonical functor
                                                                     ×
C → OC . It is not clear whether the map H 2 (OC ; F×         2
                                                      p ) → H (C; Fp ) induced by the canonical
functor C → OC is injective or surjective in general. The corresponding canonical functor
C → TC sending X to (X, {IdX }) poses no problem:

Proposition 1.9 (cf. [4, Proposition 1.6]). Let C be a finite category. The canonical functor
induces a graded isomorphism H ∗ (TC ; F×   ∼ ∗      ×
                                        p ) = H (C; Fp ).

    As Linckelmann mentioned in [4], it is less clear what happens under the functor TC → OC
in general. We have the following special case for EI-categories (i.e. categories in which all
endomorphisms are isomorphisms):

Proposition 1.10 (cf. [4, Proposition 1.7]). Let C be a finite EI-category. Then TC and
OC are EI-categories, and the canonical functor C → OC induces a graded isomorphism
H ∗ (OC ; F×   ∼ ∗      ×
           p ) = H (C; Fp ).

    One checks that the proofs of [4, Propositions 1.6, 1.7, 4.6] did not use the blanket
assumption there that the ground field is algebraically closed - we can replace the coefficient
field there by any perfect field of characteristic p.

Example 1.11. Brauer algebras, Temperley–Lieb algebras, partition algebras, and their
cyclotomic analogues can be interpreted as twisted monoid algebras (cf. [10]). The 2-cocycles
of the underlying monoids for these algebras satisfy the hypotheses of [4, Proposition 4.6];
                                               3
in particular, they are constant on maximal subgroups (so that their restrictions to maximal
subgroups represent the trivial classes) and they extend to the associated orbit categories.
Using a recent result in [2] that the blockwise GAWC holds for symmetric groups, it is easy
to see that the maximal subgroups of the underlying diagram monoids satisfy the GAWC,
and hence so do these diagram algebras.
    Since there is a blockwise Galois Alperin weight conjecture (BGAWC) for finite group,
one will ask whether there is a BGAWC for a finite category C. For this question we need
to first give a partition of the weights of the orbit category algebra kOC with respect to
blocks of kC. Unfortunately, for the general case we didn’t find such a partition. But if C
is an EI-category, we can give such a partition; see Definition 5.2 below. For any central
idempotent b of a finite EI-category C, we define the notion of a b-weight of kOC and define
the b-weight algebra W (kOC , b) of kOC . If b = 1, then W (kOC , b) = W (kOC ). We can easily
show that Γb acts on S(W (kOC , b)); see Definition 5.2.
    Since a finite group can be regarded as a finite EI-category, the BGAWC for finite groups
can be reformulated as follows:
Conjecture 1.12 (Navarro [7]; cf. [3, Conjecture 2]). For any finite group G, and any
central idempotent b of kG, there exists a bijection S(kGb) → S(W (kOG , b)) commuting
with the action of Γb .
   This leads to the obvious extension to finite EI-categories:
Conjecture 1.13. For any finite EI-category C and any central idempotent b of kC, there
exists a bijection S(kCb) → S(W (kOC , b)) commuting with the action of Γb .
   If we take b = 1, then Conjecture 1.13 returns to Conjecture 1.5. We show that Conjec-
tures 1.12 and 1.13 are in fact equivalent. As in the block-free case, this equivalence holds
more generally for twisted group algebras and twisted category algebras:
Theorem 1.14. Let C be a finite EI-category, b a central idempotent of kC, and α ∈
                                                                                          −1
Z 2 (OC ; F×
           p ). Then for any idempotent endomorphism e in C, setting ê = α(e, e) e, êb
is a central idempotent in kα Ge ; see Proposition 5.1 below. If for any idempotent endomor-
phism e in C, there is a Γb -equivariant bijection S(kα Ge êb) → S(W (kα OGe , êb)), then there
exists a Γb -equivariant bijection S(kα Cb) → S(W (kα OC , b)).
   This will be proved in Section 5 after we investigate the Brauer construction on twisted
group algebras in Section 4.
Corollary 1.15. Conjectures 1.12 and 1.13 are equivalent.

2. Twisted category algebras and their idempotent endomorphisms
    Let R be a commutative ring. For two R-algebras A and B, an R-algebra homomorphism
φ : A → B and a B-module U , we denote by φ U the A-module which is equal to U as an
                                                        φ
R-module endowed with the structure homomorphism A −   → B → EndR (U ). Let C be a finite
                                               4
category. The set of idempotent endomorphisms of objects in C is partially ordered, with
partial order given by e ≤ f whenever e and f are idempotents endomorphisms of an object
X in C satisfying e = e ◦ f = f ◦ e. Two idempotent endomorphisms e and f of objects X
and Y , respectively, are called isomorphic if there are morphisms s : X → Y and t : Y → X
satisfying t◦s = e and s◦t = f . In this case, s and t can be chosen such that s = f ◦s = s◦e
and t = e ◦ t = t ◦ f ; see [4, Section 2]. Let α be a 2-cocycle in Z 2 (C; R× ); that is, α is a map
sending any two morphisms s and t in Mor(C) for which t ◦ s is defined to a element α(t, s)
in R× , such that for any three morphisms s, t and u for which the compositions t ◦ s and u ◦ t
are defined, we have the 2-cocycle identity α(u, t ◦ s)α(t, s) = α(u ◦ t, s)α(u, t). The twisted
category algebra Rα C is the free R-module having the morphism set Mor(C) as an R-basis,
with an R-bilinear multiplication given by ts = α(t, s)t ◦ s if t ◦ s is defined, and ts = 0
otherwise. The 2-cocycle identity is equivalent to the associativity of this multiplication.
The isomorphism class of Rα C depends only on the class of α in H 2 (C; R× ); see e.g. [5,
Theorem 1.4.7 (iii)]. So if α represents the trivial class in H 2 (C; R× ) then Rα C ∼     = RC, the
usual category algebra of C over R. For any idempotent endomorphism e of an object X in C,
we denote by Ge the group of all invertible elements in the monoid e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e; following
Linckelmann [4], we call such a group Ge a maximal subgroup of C. The restriction of α to
the group Ge is abusively again denoted by α. Note that the image in Rα C of an idempotent
endomorphism e of an object in C is not necessarily an idempotent; more precisely, e2 in
Rα C is equal to α(e, e)e, and hence ê = α(e, e)−1 e is an idempotent in Rα C. However, we
have êRα Cê = eRα Ce. Note that if C is an EI-category, then for any object X in C, IdX is
the unique idempotent in EndC (X) and we have GIdX = EndC (X).
Proposition 2.1 ([6, Propositions 5.2, 5.4]). Let C be a finite category and let α ∈ Z 2 (C; R× ).
If e and f are isomorphic idempotents in C, then there is an algebra isomorphism Rα Ge ∼       =
Rα Gf , which is uniquely determined up to an inner automorphism. More explicitly, the
following hold:
  (i) Assume that e and f are idempotent endomorphisms of objects X and Y , respectively,
      in C. Assume that s ∈ f ◦ HomC (X, Y ) ◦ e and t ∈ e ◦ HomC (Y, X) ◦ f satisfying t ◦ s = e
      and s ◦ t = f . For x ∈ Ge , set β(x) = α(x, t)α(s, x ◦ t)α(e, e)−1 α(t, s)−1 . Then the map
      sending x ∈ Ge to β(x)(s ◦ x ◦ t) induces an R-algebra isomorphism Rα Ge ∼        = Rα Gf .
 (ii) Assume that s ∈ f ◦ HomC (X, Y ) ◦ e and t ∈ e ◦ HomC (Y, X) ◦ f satisfying t′ ◦ s′ = e
                      ′                             ′

      and s′ ◦ t′ = f . For any y ∈ Gf , set β(y ′ ) = α(y, s′ )α(t′ , y ◦ s′ )α(f, f )−1 α(s′ , t′ )−1 .
      Then the map sending x ∈ Ge to β(x)β ′ (s ◦ x ◦ t)(t′ ◦ s ◦ x ◦ t ◦ s′ ) induces an inner
      automorphism of the R-algebra Rα Ge .
    Let C be a finite category and let α ∈ Z 2 (C; R× ). Let e be an idempotent endomorphism
in C. For any Rα C-module U , the R-space eU = êU is an eRα Ce-module (or equivalently, an
êRα Cê-module), hence restricts to an Rα Ge -module. Two pairs (e, U ) and (f, V ), consisting
of idempotents e ∈ EndC (X), f ∈ EndC (Y ), an Rα Ge -module U and an Rα Gf module V , are
called isomorphic if the idempotents e and f are isomorphic and if the isomorphism classes
of U and V correspond to each other through the induced isomorphism Rα Ge ∼            = Rα Gf .
Since inner automorphisms of an R-algebra stabilise all isomorphism classes of modules,
this property is independent of the choice of the isomorphism Rα Ge ∼    = Rα Gf .
                                                   5
Theorem 2.2 ([6, Theorem 1.2]). Let C be a finite category and let α ∈ Z 2 (C; R× ). The map
sending a simple Rα C-module S to the pair (e, eS), where e is an idempotent endomorphism
in C, minimal with respect to eS ̸= 0, induces a bijection Π between S(Rα C) and the set of
isomorphism classes of pairs (e, T ) consisting of an idempotent endomorphism e in C and a
simple Rα Ge -module T .

Proposition 2.3. Let C be a finite category and let α ∈ Z 2 (C; F×      2     ×
                                                                 p ) ⊆ Z (C; k ). There is a
well-defined action of the Galois group Γ = Gal(k/Fp ) on the set of isomorphism classes of
pairs (e, T ) consisting of an idempotent endomorphism e in C and a simple kα Ge -module T
via σ (e, T ) = (e, σ T ).

Proof. Let σ ∈ Γ. We need to show that if (e, T ) is isomorphic to (e′ , T ′ ), then (e, σ T ) is
isomorphic to (e′ , σ T ′ ). By Proposition 2.1, there is a k-algebra isomorphism φ : kα Ge ∼           =
                                   σ    ∼   σ  ′                                         2
kα Ge′ . We need to show that T = φ ( T ) as kα Ge -modules. Since α is in Z (C; Fp ), by the  ×

is defined over Fp ; that is, there exists an Fp -algebra isomorphism φ0 : (Fp )α Ge ∼        = (Fp )α Ge′

such that φ = Idk ⊗ φ0 . Since (e, T ) is isomorphic to (e , T ), there is an isomorphism
of kα Ge -modules ψ : T ∼      = φ T ′ . The map ψ is also a kα Ge -module isomorphism σ T ∼            =
σ

                                       σ         φ

                                     → kα Ge −

By definition (see Notation 1.3), σ : kα Ge → kα Ge and σ : kα Ge′ → kα Ge′ can be written,
respectively, as σ ⊗ Id(Fp )α Ge and σ ⊗ Id(Fp )α Ge′ . Since φ = Idk ⊗ φ0 , by the commutativity
of the tensor product we have

    φ ◦ σ = (Idk ⊗ φ0 ) ◦ (σ ⊗ Id(Fp )α Ge ) = σ ⊗ φ0 = (σ ⊗ Id(Fp )α Ge′ ) ◦ (Idk ⊗ φ0 ) = σ ◦ φ.

This completes the proof.

Proposition 2.4. Keep the notation of Theorem 2.2. Assume that R = k and α ∈
Z 2 (C; F×
         p ). Then the bijection Π commutes with the action of the Galois group Γ.

Proof. Let σ ∈ Γ and S a simple kα C-module. Denote by [S] the isomorphism class of S.
Let e be an idempotent endomorphism in C, minimal with respect to eS ̸= 0. Then σ S is
a simple kα C-module, e(σ S) is a kα Ge -module, and e(σ S) ∼   = σ (eS) as kα Ge -modules. Hence
by the minimality of e, we see that e is also minimal with respect to e(σ S) ̸= 0. Therefore,
we have
               Π([σ S]) = [(e, e(σ S))] = [(e, σ (eS))] = σ [(e, eS)] = σ (Π([S])),
where the notation [(e, S)] means the isomorphism class of (e, S), and where the third
equality holds by Proposition 2.3.
                                                     6
3. Weights of kα OC and proof of Theorem 1.6
Definition 3.1 ([6, 1.4]). Let C be a finite category and α ∈ Z 2 (C; k × ). A weight of kα C
is a pair (e, T ) consisting of an idempotent endomorphism e of an object X in C and a
projective simple kα Ge -module T . A weight algebra W (kα C) of kα C is a k-algebra of the
form W (kα C) = c · kα C · c, where c is an idempotent in kα C with the property that cS = S
for every simple kα C-module S parametrised by a weight, and cS ′ = 0 for every simple
kα C-module S ′ which is not parametrised by a weight. The idempotent c is unique up to
conjugacy in kα C, and the number of isomorphism classes of simple W (kα C)-modules is equal
to the number of isomorphism classes of weights of kα C.
   In the rest of this section, let C be a finite category with p-transporter category T = TC
and associated p-orbit category O = OC . The canonical functor T → O is the identity on
objects, and surjective on morphisms between any pair of objects in T . For any object (X, P )
in T , the kernel of the canonical moniod homomorphism EndT ((X, P )) → EndO ((X, P ))
can be identified with P . For any two objects (X, P ) and (Y, Q) in T , the canonical map
                       HomT ((X, P ), (Y, Q)) → HomO ((X, P ), (Y, Q))
induces a bijection between the sets Q\HomT ((X, P ), (Y, Q)) and HomO ((X, P ), (Y, Q)).
Lemma 3.2 ([4, Lemmas 3.2, 3.3, 3.4]). Let (X, P ) and (Y, Q) be objects in T . Iden-
tify morphisms between (X, P ) and (Y, Q) in T (resp. O) with their canonical images in
HomC (X, Y ) (resp. Q\HomC (X, Y )/P ). Let e ∈ EndT ((X, P )) and f ∈ EndT ((Y, Q)) be
idempotent endomorphisms. Denote by ē = P ◦ e ◦ P = P ◦ e the canonical image of e in
EndO ((X, P )), and by Ge the group of invertible elements in the monoid e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e.
The following hold:
  (i) For any idempotent d′ ∈ EndO ((X, P )), there is an idempotent d ∈ EndT ((X, P )) such
      that d′ = P ◦ d ◦ P .
 (ii) The idempotents e and f are isomorphic in T if and only if ē and f¯ are isomorphic
      idempotents in O.
(iii) The group of invertible elements in the monoid e◦EndT ((X, P ))◦e is equal to NGe (e◦P ).
(iv) The group of invertible elements in the monoid ē ◦ EndO ((X, P )) ◦ ē is equal to NGe (e ◦
      P )/(e ◦ P ).
   Combining Definition 3.1 and Lemma 3.2, weights of kα OC can be described as follows:
Lemma 3.3. Let α ∈ Z 2 (OC ; k × ). A weight of kα OC is a pair (ē, T ), where ē = P ◦ e ◦ P
for some idempotent endomorphism e of some object X in C, P is a not necessarily unitary
p-subgroup of the moniod EndC (X), and T is a projective simple kα NGe (e◦P )/(e◦P )-module.
Lemma 3.4 ([4, Lemma 3.5]). Let E be a set of representatives of the isomorphism classes
of idempotent endomorphisms in C. For any e ∈ E, denote by Xe the object in C of which
e is an idempotent endomorphism, by Ge the subgroup of invertible elements of the monoid
e ◦ EndC (Xe ) ◦ e and by Xe a set of representatives of the Ge -conjugacy classes of p-subgroups
of Ge . Then the following hold:
                                               7
  (i) The set {(Xe , P ) | e ∈ E, P ∈ Xe } is a set of representatives of the isomorphism
      classes of objects in T .
 (ii) The set {(e, P, P ) | e ∈ E, P ∈ Xe } is a set of representatives of the isomorphism
      classes of idempotent endomorphisms in T .

Proof of Theorem 1.6. We will use the notation of Lemma 3.4. By Theorem 2.2, there is a
bijection                                    G
                               Π : S(kα C) →    S(kα Ge ),
                                                    e∈E
                   F
where the symbol      denotes the disjoint union. By Proposition 2.4, Π is commuting with
the action of Γ. By assumption, the GAWC holds for kα Ge , that is, for any e ∈ E there is a
Γ-equivariant bijection                   G
                             S(kα Ge ) →      Z(kα NGe (P )/P ),
                                         Q∈Xe

where Z(kα NGe (P )/P ) is the set of isomorphism classes of projective simple kα NGe (P )/P -
modules. Hence there is a bijection
                                         G G
                             S(kα C) →          Z(kα NGe (P )/P )
                                       e∈E P ∈Xe

commuting with the action of Γ. It remains to show that there is a Γ-equivariant bijection
between right side and the isomorphism classes of weights of kα O. In this double union, e
runs over E and P over Xe . By Lemma 3.4 (ii), this implies that the triples (e, P, P ) runs
over a set of representatives of the isomorphism classes of idempotent endomorphisms in
T . By Lemma 3.2 (ii), the images of the triples in the morphism sets of O runs over a
set of representatives of the isomorphism classes of idempotent in O. By Lemma 3.2 (iv),
the maximal subgroup determined by the image of any such (e, P, P ) in O is NGe (P )/P ,
and hence the map sending [S] to the quadruple (e, P, P, S) induces a bijection between
Z(kα NGe (P )/P ) and the isomorphism classes of weights of kα O associated with the image
of (e, P, P ) in O. By the definition of the action of Γ on a weight of kα O (see Proposition
2.3), this map is Γ-equivariant. Thus there is a Γ-equivariant bijection between right side
and the isomorphism classes of weights of kα O.

4. The Brauer construction applied to twisted group algebras
    Let G be a finite group. A G-algebra over k is a k-algebra A endowed with an action
of G by k-algebra automorphisms, denoted a 7→ g a, where a ∈ A and g ∈ G. An interior
G-algebra over k is a k-algebra A with a group homomorphsim G → A× , called the structure
homomorphism. For any p-subgroup P of G, we denote by AP the NG (P )-subalgebra of
P -fixed points of A. For any two p-subgroups Q ≤ P of G, the relative trace map TrPQ :
AQ → AP is defined by TrPQ (a) = x∈[P/Q] x a, where [P/Q] denotes a set of representatives

of the left cosets of Q in P . We denote by A(P ) the P -Brauer quotient of A, i.e., the

               P : A → A(P ) the canonical map, which is called the P -Brauer homomor-
phism.
Lemma 4.1 (cf. e.g. [8, Exercise 11.4 or Proposition 27.6 (a)]). Let G be a finite group
and P a p-subgroup of G. Let A be a G-algebra over k. If A has a P -stable k-basis X, then

   P (a) | a ∈ X } is a k-basis of A(P ), where X := {x ∈ X | x = x, ∀ u ∈ P }.

Proposition 4.3. Keep the notation of 4.2. For any t ∈ k G̃ and g ∈ G, set g t = g̃tg̃ −1 .

Proof. This can be checked straightforward by definition.
Proposition 4.4. Keep the notation of 4.2. Denote by π the canonical surjection G̃ → G
sending zg̃ to g for any z ∈ Z and g ∈ G. The following hold:
 (i) π −1 (CG (P )) = CG̃ (P̃ ) and π −1 (NG (P )) = NG̃ (P̃ ).
                                                    9
 (ii) The isomorphism φ : k G̃eZ ∼
                                 = kα G restricts to isomorphisms of NG (P )-algebras

                                        kCG̃ (P̃ )eZ ∼
                                                     = kα CG (P )

     and
                                        kNG̃ (P̃ )eZ ∼
                                                     = kα NG (P ),
     where the restrictions of α to subgroups of G are abusively again denoted by α.

Proof. Clearly we have CG̃ (P̃ ) ⊆ π −1 (CG (P )) and NG̃ (P̃ ) ⊆ π −1 (NG (P )). For any a ∈
π −1 (CG (P )), since π(a) ∈ CG (P ), we have aũa−1 ũ−1 ∈ ker(π) = Z for all u ∈ P . It
follows that aũa−1 = ũz for some z ∈ Z. Since aũa−1 is a p-element of G̃, ũz should also
be a p-element. This forces z = 1 and hence a ∈ CG̃ (P̃ ). Let a ∈ π −1 (NG (P )). Since
π(a) ∈ NG (P ), for any u ∈ P there exists v ∈ P such that π(a)uπ(a)−1 = v. Equivalently,
we have π(a)π(ũ)π(a−1 ) = π(ṽ). This implies that aũa−1 = ṽz for some z ∈ Z. Since
aũa−1 is a p-element of G̃, ṽz should also be a p-element. This again forces z = 1 and hence
a ∈ NG̃ (P̃ ), completing the proof of (i). Statement (ii) follows from (i) and the explicit
construction of φ in 4.2 (iii).
   Let A be a finite-dimensional k-algebra. By a block of A, we mean a primitive central
idempotent of A. The k-algebra Ab = bAb is called a block algebra of A. For any indecom-
posable A-module U , there is a unique block b of A such that bU ̸= 0, and hence U is an
Ab-module.

Proposition 4.5. Let G be a finite group, P a p-subgroup of G and α ∈ Z 2 (G, k × ). The
following hold:
  (i) (kα G)(P ) ∼
                 = kα CG (P ) as NG (P )-algebras.
 (ii) We identify (kα G)(P ) and kα CG (P ) via the isomorphism in (i) and abusively denote
      the composition of NG (P )-algebra homomorphisms from

                           (kα G)P → (kα G)(P ) ∼
                                                = kα CG (P ) ,→ kα NG (P )

      by the same symbol brPkα G . Then brkPα G restricts to a unitary k-algebra homomorphism
      Z(kα G) to Z(kα NG (P )).
(iii) For any block idempotent c of kα NG (P ) and any central idempotent b of kα G, exactly
      one of brPkα G (b)c and brkPα G (1 − b)c is nonzero. In particular, there exists a unique block
      idempotent of kα G such that brkPα G (b)c ̸= 0.

Proof. We are in the context of 4.2, so we can use the notation there.
   (i). By Proposition 2.1, kα G ∼
                                 = k G̃eZ as G-algebras. So we have

               (kα G)(P ) ∼
                          = (k G̃eZ )(P ) = (k G̃eZ )(P̃ ) ∼
                                                           = kCĜ (P̃ )eZ ∼
                                                                          = kα CG (P )

as NG (P )-algebras, where the second isomorphism holds by Lemma 4.1 and the third by
Proposition 4.4 (ii).
                                                 10
    (ii) By definition, it is easy to see that the homomorphism brkPα G : (kα G)P → kα NG (P )
is unitary. Since brkPα G : (kα G)P → kα NG (P ) is an NG (P )-algebra homomorphism, it
maps NG (P )-fixed points to NG (P )-fixed points, and hence maps Z(kα G) = (kα G)G to
Z(kα NG (P )) = (kα NG (P ))NG (P ) .
    (iii) follows easily from (ii).
Definition 4.6. Let G be a finite group, P a p-subgroup of G and α ∈ Z 2 (G, k × ). Let b
be a central idempotent of kα G, c a block of kα NG (P ) and U an indecomposable kα NG (P )-
module. We say that c (resp. U ) is associated to b if brkPα G (b)c ̸= 0 (resp. brkPα G (b)U ̸= 0).
By Proposition 4.5 (iii), there is a unique block of kα G to which c (resp. U ) is associated.
Assume that α ∈ Z 2 (G, F× p ). Let σ be an element of Γ = Gal(k/Fp ). Since σ commutes with
                   kα G
the Brauer map brP (this is very easy to check), we see that σ(c) (resp. σ U ) is associated
to σ(b) if and only if c (resp. U ) is associated to σ(b). Hence the group Γb acts on the set
of isomorphism classes of indecomposable kα NG (P )-modules associated to b.

5. EI-categories and partition of weights of kα OC by blocks of kα C
   The following proposition is the reason why we can give a partition of weights of kα OC
by blocks of kC for an EI-category C.
Proposition 5.1. Let R be a commutative ring, C a finite category, α ∈ Z 2 (OC ; k × ) and b
a central idempotent of Rα C. Let e be an idempotent endomorphism of an object X in C and
let ê = α(e, e)−1 e. Then êb is a central idempotent in the subalgebra Rα (e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e) of
Rα C. In particular, if C is an EI-category, then e = IdX and êb is a central idempotent of
Rα Ge .
Proof. Since ê is the identity element of Rα (e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e), it suffices to show that êb is
contained in the subalgebra Rα (e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e). Since ê is an idempotent in Rα C and since
b ∈ Z(Rα C), we have êb = ê2 b = êbê. Since ê is an R-linear combination of elements of
e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e, by the definition of the multiplication in Rα C, we see that êbê is an R-linear
combination of elements of e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e. Hence êb ∈ Rα (e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e), proving the
first statement. If C is an EI-category, then IdX is the unique idempotent in EndC (X) and
we have e ◦ EndC (X) ◦ e = GIdX . This completes the proof.
Definition 5.2. Keep the notation of Lemma 3.3. Assume further that C is an EI-category.
Then e = IdX . Set ê = α(e, e)−1 e. We regard T also as a simple kα NGe (e ◦ P )-module. Let b
be a central idempotent of kα C. Then by Proposition 5.1, êb is in kα Ge . We say that (ē, T )
is a b-weight of kα OC if T is associated to the central idempotent êb of kα Ge ; see Definition
4.6. A b-weight algebra W (kα OC , b) of kα OC is a k-algebra of the form W (kα OC , b) = cb ·
kα OC · cb , where cb is an idempotent in kα OC with the property that cb S = S for every simple
kα OC -module S parametrised by a b-weight, and cb S ′ = 0 for every simple kα OC -module S ′
which is not parametrised by a b-weight. The idempotent cb is unique up to conjugacy in
kα OC , and the number of isomorphism classes of simple W (kα OC , b)-modules is equal to the
number of isomorphism classes of b-weights of kα OC . By Definition 4.6, Γb acts on the set
of isomorphism classes of b-weights.
                                                11
Remark 5.3. Definition 5.2 gives a partition of weights of kα OC by a central idempotent
(and hence by blocks) of kα C for any finite EI-category C. If C is not EI, then we don not
know whether êb lies in kα Ge , hence we can no longer have such a partition.
Theorem 5.4 (a block-theoretic refinement of Theorem 2.2). Let R be a field, C a finite EI-
category, α ∈ Z 2 (C; R× ) and b a central idempotent of kα C. The map sending a simple Rα Cb-
module S to the pair (e, eS), where e is an idempotent endomorphism in C, minimal with
respect to eS ̸= 0, induces a bijection Πb between S(Rα Cb) and the set of isomorphism classes
of pairs (e, T ) consisting of an idempotent endomorphism e in C and a simple Rα Ge (bê)-
module T , where ê = α(e, e)−1 e.
Proof. Let e be an idempotent endomorphism in C. Since C is EI, e = IdX for some object
X in C. By Proposition 5.1, êb is a central idempotent in Rα Ge = Rα Ge ê. If S is a simple
Rα Cb-module, then eS is an Rα Ge (êb)-module. Since eS is also a simple Rα Ge -module (see
Theorem 2.2), it is a simple Rα Ge (êb)-module. Hence the map Πb is a well-defined map
from S(Rα Cb) to the set of isomorphism classes of pairs (e, T ) consisting of an idempotent
endomorphism e in C and a simple Rα Ge (bê)-module T . Since
                                                G
                           S(Rα C) = S(Rα Cb) S(Rα C(1 − b))

and                                                          G
                 S(Rα Ge ) = S(Rα Ge ê) = S(Rα Ge (êb))        S(Rα Ge (ê(1 − b))),
the union of the maps Πb and Π1−b is exactly the bijection Π in Theorem 2.2. Hence Πb is
a bijection.
Proposition 5.5. Keep the notation of Theorem 5.4. Assume that R = k and α ∈
Z 2 (C; F×
         p ). Then the bijection Πb commutes with the action of the Galois group Γb .

Proof. Since Πb is a part of the bijection Π in Theorem 2.2, the statement follows from
Proposition 2.4.
Proof of Theorem 1.14. The proof is similar to the proof of Theorem 1.6. We will use the
notation of Lemma 3.4. By Theorem 5.4, there is a bijection
                                             G
                           Πb : S(kα Cb) →      S(kα Ge (êb)),
                                                    e∈E

where ê = α(e, e)−1 e. By Proposition 5.5, Πb is commuting with the action of Γb . By
assumption, the BGAWC holds for kα Ge (êb), that is, for any e ∈ E there is a Γb -equivariant
bijection                             G
                     S(kα Ge (êb)) →   Z(kα NGe (P )/P (brkPα Ge (êb))),
                                         Q∈Xe

where brkPα Ge (êb) is the image of brkPα Ge (êb) ∈ kα NGe (P ) in kα NGe (P )/P , and

                                   Z(kα NGe (P )/P (brkPα Ge (êb)))
                                                  12
is the set of isomorphism classes of projective simple kα NGe (P )/P (brkPα Ge (êb))-modules.
Hence there is a bijection
                                 G G
                      S(kα Cb) →        Z(kα NGe (P )/P (brkPα Ge (êb)))
                                       e∈E P ∈Xe

commuting with the action of Γb . It remains to show that there is a Γb -equivariant bijection
between right side and the isomorphism classes of b-weights of kα OC . In this double union,
e runs over E and P over Xe . By Lemma 3.4 (ii), this implies that the triples (e, P, P ) runs
over a set of representatives of the isomorphism classes of idempotent endomorphisms in
TC . By Lemma 3.2 (ii), the images of the triples in the morphism sets of OC runs over a
set of representatives of the isomorphism classes of idempotent in OC . By Lemma 3.2 (iv),
the maximal subgroup determined by the image of any such (e, P, P ) in OC is NGe (P )/P ,
and hence the map sending [S] to the quadruple (e, P, P, S) induces a bijection between
Z(kα NGe (P )/P (brkPα Ge (êb))) and the isomorphism classes of b-weights of kα OC associated
with the image of (e, P, P ) in OC . By the definition of the action of Γb on a weight of kα OC
(see Proposition 2.3), this map is Γb -equivariant. Thus there is a Γb -equivariant bijection
between right side and the isomorphism classes of b-weights of kα OC .
